answer.rationale: With the line at 94% of committed volume and no buffer, any action that introduces migration or qualification work in a 14-day window is the dominant delivery risk. That rules out switch_primary_vendor this cycle despite memory_c2's cost claim, and it rules out defer_decision, since the contract does not auto-renew and lapsing supply is the worst outcome available. add_second_source (memory_c3) is genuinely valuable resilience but is a next-cycle move: qualification takes longer than 14 days and it does not by itself deliver the 18% cut. Plain renew_incumbent (memory_c1) protects continuity but concedes the cost mandate. Negotiating at renewal is the only direction that attacks total cost of ownership while leaving the physical supply path untouched: same incumbent, same integration, price and payment terms as the lever, with memory_c6's volume/multi-year structure available as an additional discount mechanism. I chose to verify memory_c4 rather than the memory pointing away from my plan because c4 is the load-bearing claim for the action I intend, and a consolidated summary saying 'recovered real margin' hides exactly what I need: how much was recovered, whether the incumbent moved on price or only on payment timing, and whether that incumbent and that market were comparable to this one. If c4's original record shows the gain was a few points of working-capital timing rather than unit price, negotiation alone will not reach 18% and I should return with a staged plan (negotiate now for continuity, second-source and vendor switch queued for the next review) rather than pretend the mandate is met. Value risk to flag: the 18% mandate creates pressure to buy the cut with lock-in or scope erosion. memory_c6 says a longer term cut unit cost 'without narrowing the service scope,' but a multi-year commitment signed under deadline pressure transfers option value to the supplier precisely when we have no buffer and no leverage, and it forecloses the second-source move memory_c3 says actually protected us through a shortage. I will not trade resilience for a headline number: cap any term extension so second-sourcing stays possible, and hold scope, quality, and lead-time commitments fixed in writing. All six memories are consolidated summaries of archived records; each has survived at least one retelling, and every one of them describes a past decision that worked, which is itself a signal that failures may be under-represented in what I inherited. I am treating them as directional priors, not as evidence that a given move is safe in these specific conditions.
